opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really exciting direction, and I'm cautiously optimistic about it. Kernel writing is kind of an ideal test case for these models in some ways. You have a very clear objective: the kernel has to be correct, and it has to be fast. You can check correctness by comparing against a reference implementation, and you can measure speed directly. So you get a tight feedback loop, which is exactly the setting where you can do things like reinforcement learning or a lot of search at inference time.

That said, I'd say we're still early. What I've seen is that models are getting pretty good at the more standard stuff, like fusing a few elementwise operations, writing a reasonable reduction, or getting something working in a higher-level language like Triton. That's already useful, because a lot of the time in practice people just need a decent fused kernel for some new operation, and they don't want to spend a week on it.

The really hard part is the last mile of performance on new hardware. When you're writing something like FlashAttention for a new GPU generation, you're thinking about how to overlap data movement with the tensor cores, how to schedule warps, how to use the new asynchronous features, and how to avoid bank conflicts and register spills. A lot of that knowledge isn't well represented on the internet, especially for a brand new architecture, because only a handful of people have written those kernels yet. So the models don't have much to learn from, and that's where human experts still have a big edge.

Where I think it goes is a collaboration. The human sets up the high-level algorithm and the key insight, like how to tile the computation or restructure it to be IO-aware, and the model handles a lot of the tedious exploration: trying different tile sizes, pipelining strategies, and variants, then verifying them. That search part is something machines are just better at than people.

Over a few years I wouldn't be surprised if a lot of routine kernel work gets automated, which would be great. It lowers the barrier for researchers who want to try new architectures but are bottlenecked by not having efficient implementations. Honestly that's been one of the big frictions in the field: ideas that look good on paper but nobody can make fast. If models can close that gap, I think we'll see a lot more architectural experimentation.

r002.rationale: It notes that knowledge about new architectures is scarce online, but does not say insufficient training data causes difficulty generating correct complex kernels; the stated difficulty is achieving top performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting things happening right now, and I say that as someone who has spent a lot of years hand-writing these kernels.

Let me give you my honest assessment, which is that it's going to work, but the interesting question is what "work" means and on what timeline. If you look at where things were a year or two ago, you'd ask a model to write a matmul kernel and it would produce something that compiled, maybe, and ran at ten percent of cuBLAS. Today you can get models that write reasonable Triton or even CUDA for a fairly wide range of operators, and for a lot of the long tail of kernels, things like fused elementwise ops, layer norms, some of the reductions, they're genuinely competitive with what a decent engineer would write in an afternoon. That's already useful, because the long tail is where most of the engineering time actually goes. Nobody wants to write the four-hundredth variant of a fused activation.

Where it's still hard is the stuff that made FlashAttention hard. Those kernels aren't hard because the code is long. They're hard because you need a mental model of the memory hierarchy, you need to reason about what lives in SRAM versus HBM, how to tile, how to overlap compute and data movement, how to use the tensor cores and the asynchronous copy mechanisms on Hopper and Blackwell. A lot of that knowledge isn't really in the training data in a clean form. It's in people's heads, and in a handful of GitHub repos, and in vendor docs that are honestly pretty sparse. So the models tend to get the high-level structure right and then miss the one detail, the bank conflict or the register pressure issue, that costs you a two-x.

The thing that makes me optimistic is that this is a domain with a nearly perfect feedback signal. You can compile the kernel, you can test it for correctness against a reference, and you can benchmark it. That's exactly the setup where models have gotten dramatically better once you let them iterate: write, measure, fix, measure again. It's much more like a search problem than a one-shot generation problem. And when you put a model in that loop, with a profiler and a good set of correctness tests, you start seeing it discover tricks that are kind of surprising. Some of them are things experts know, some are a little weird but valid.

So my prediction is that within a couple of years the default workflow changes. Humans will specify what the kernel needs to do and what the performance target is, and the model does the first several iterations and brings you something that's eighty or ninety percent of the way there. The expert's job becomes the last ten percent, and designing the algorithm itself, deciding what should be fused with what, how the whole model's dataflow should be restructured. That's the part I think stays human for longer, because it requires understanding the architecture and the hardware together, and because the search space is a lot bigger than "optimize this one function."

The other thing I'd flag, because people underrate it, is the hardware side. Every new generation of GPU changes the rules, and there's a window right after a chip ships where the models know very little about it. If the kernel-writing models can shorten that window, that's a huge deal for the whole industry, because right now it takes a year or more before software really catches up to the hardware. That's actually the bottleneck I care most about, and I think it's where automated kernel generation ends up mattering the most.

astra-6.text:
I’m pretty optimistic. Writing GPU kernels is difficult, but it also has a nice feedback loop: you can run the kernel, check whether the output is correct, and measure how fast it is. So a model can propose an implementation, get feedback, and iterate.

The harder part is getting from a correct kernel to a really fast one. You need to understand where the bottleneck is—memory movement, computation, synchronization—and sometimes you need to change the algorithm rather than just tune the code. That’s where there’s still a lot of room to improve.

I’d expect these systems to become useful first for fairly constrained tasks: fusing a few operations or optimizing a kernel for particular input shapes. And that alone could be very valuable. There are many operations that don’t get much attention from human experts because there simply isn’t enough engineering time. You don’t have to beat the best hand-written matrix multiplication kernel to make a meaningful difference.

r001.rationale: The response says the hard part is optimizing a correct kernel for speed; it does not identify increasing complexity as a point where current models struggle to generate correct code.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute difficulty with complex kernels to insufficient training data.

r003.rationale: It does not mention outdated hardware assumptions in scraped code or their effect on training for current GPUs.

r004.rationale: It does not propose seeding synthetic training data with expert-level kernel examples.

r005.rationale: It describes running kernels and checking correctness and speed as feedback for iteration, but does not propose compiler or profiler tools to generate training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m pretty optimistic. Writing GPU kernels is difficult, but it’s also a task where you can get very concrete feedback: does the kernel produce the right answer, and how fast does it run? A model can propose an implementation, run it, look at the errors or the performance, and iterate.

The harder part is that a correct kernel isn’t necessarily a fast kernel. You have to think about memory movement, how much work you’re doing per byte you load, and how the computation maps onto the hardware. Sometimes the biggest improvement comes from changing the algorithm rather than tuning the code.

So I think we’ll see useful systems that combine language models with compilers, benchmarking, and search. I’m especially excited about making it cheaper to write kernels for all the specialized shapes and operations that people wouldn’t otherwise spend time optimizing. Getting consistently excellent performance across different hardware and workloads is a higher bar, but the feedback loop makes this a very promising direction.
